title: presentation with python plot
text:
import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

plt.close("all")

import statsmodels.api as sm

mtcars = sm.datasets.get_rdataset("mtcars").data
X = sm.add_constant(mtcars["wt"])
y = mtcars["mpg"]
model = sm.OLS(y, X).fit()

# 2. Setup Figure
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(10, 5))

# Plot the points (open circles like R)
ax.scatter(model.fittedvalues, model.resid, facecolors='none', edgecolors='black')

# Add the horizontal 'zero' line
ax.axhline(0, color='silver', linestyle=':', zorder=0)

# 3. Add the Red Lowess Line (The 'R' special)
lowess = sm.nonparametric.lowess(model.resid, model.fittedvalues, frac=2/3)
ax.plot(lowess[:, 0], lowess[:, 1], color='red', lw=1, alpha=0.8)

# 4. Label the Top 3 Outliers
# Find indices of the 3 largest absolute residuals
top_3_idx = np.abs(model.resid).sort_values(ascending=False).head(3).index

for i in top_3_idx:
    ax.annotate(i, (model.fittedvalues[i], model.resid[i]), 
                xytext=(5, 5), textcoords='offset points', fontsize=9)

# Formatting
ax.set_title("Residuals vs Fitted")
ax.set_xlabel("Fitted values")
ax.set_ylabel("Residuals")
plt.savefig("01_residuals_vs_fitted.png")







Figure 1: Residuals vs Fitted Plot

Flying Over Stats 20

OutlineWorkflow (in research)Workflow (in workplaces)What is R?


Over the next 10 weeks, we will try to cover the following topics:

Data Science Workflow (computational steps), Reproducibility, Communication.

Core/Base R (the language, data structures, functions, etc.).

Data Wrangling (not analyzable -> analyzable).

Debugging/Problem Solving.
Tidyverse + Data Viz

Distributions, Sampling, Statistics.
Control Flow, Functions, and Programming Concepts.
Linear Algebra in R.






A Data Science Workflow







From Google




From CRAN (the Comprehensive R Archive Network):

R is a system for statistical computation and graphics. It consists of a language plus a run-time environment with graphics, a debugger, access to certain system functions, and the ability to run programs stored in script files.

Translation:

R is a language with an interpreter and a standard library (toolkit/toolbox of functions)
With execution support code (behind the scenes code that helps your R code run on your computer)
All for the practice of statistics (involves computation,simulation, data visualization etc.)

R can also monitor/analyze code, identify coding errors, interact with your operating system, run programs saved on your computer as scripts (or similar) among other things.

title: Lecture 01
text:
Activity #2 Takeaways

In the beginning, R is like a calculator
Numbers, operators, vectors, data frames, functions are objects.

A simplification: virtually everything in R is an object.
Names like x, y, z, iris, rivers are associated with R objects and by calling the name, we have access.
The fundamental data structure in R is the vector
Vectors are indexed (elements are numbered 1 to however many elements we have)

title: Lecture 01
text:
Why R and not Python?

The basic difference: R was built by statisticians for statisticians, so the focus is narrower.
Python was built by software engineers for general purpose applications, so the focus is broad.
R is great for focusing on thinking about statistical problems, solving them, and communicating the results
Python is great for doing lots of different things. Example, download thousands of YouTube videos, analyze the images frame by frame, transcribe the sound into words, analyze the data, etc.

title: Lecture 01
text:
Why R and not Python? (cont’d)

R is “Problem-First” or “Problem-Forward”
In R, data structures are integrated directly into the language and do not require additional tools (but tools, found in libraries, are helpful).
When you load a dataset, R assumes you want to analyze it. The syntax is designed to mirror the way a researcher thinks: “I want to study something which involves data, get the data, then filter/subset it, then group it, then summarize/describe, then model, etc.”

Also R’s simpler modeling formulas allows one to remain thinking about the analytical problem.

title: Lecture 01
text:
Why R and not Python? (cont’d)

Python is “System-First”
In Python, you “build” your environment before you can solve the problem (importing tools, found in libraries such as pandas, numpy, etc.)
In Python, it matters how your programming code integrates within a larger system, the result is versatility. So it is easy for Python to interact with YouTube for example (not as easy/or maybe not possible in R)
In R, what matters is how the programming code helps you reveal the truth found in the data.

R has “built-in” data “data = mtcars”, Python does not, need a library.
In both situations, we are testing the same hypothesis: does MPG change in a predictable direction as WT changes?
Notice the “<-” in R this is called a “gets”, it is used for assignment. Could read it as “model 1 gets”
Python uses “=” for both assignment and options
You can use “=” for assignment in R, but it is really meant to identify options
R is written in a way comparable to how we think about things in statistics lm(mpg ~ wt, data = mtcars) lm() is the basic linear model FUNCTION (important word) and the () encloses its “arguments”. Functions do all of the “work” in R.
~ could be read “as a function of” so we can read the code like “linear model(mpg as a function of wt the data is mtcars)” and “model1” “gets” the result.
You don’t need to print() explicitly in R, but you must explicity print() in Python to see results

import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import statsmodels.api as sm

mtcars = sm.datasets.get_rdataset("mtcars").data
X = sm.add_constant(mtcars["wt"])
y = mtcars["mpg"]
model = sm.OLS(y, X).fit()

fitted = model.fittedvalues
residuals = model.resid

influence = model.get_influence()
standardized_resid = influence.resid_studentized_internal
leverage = influence.hat_matrix_diag
cooks = influence.cooks_distance[0]

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(8, 5), dpi=100)

ax.scatter(model.fittedvalues, model.resid, alpha=0.7)
ax.axhline(0, color='red', linestyle='--')
ax.set_xlabel("Fitted values")
ax.set_ylabel("Residuals")
ax.set_title("Residuals vs Fitted")
plt.tight_layout()




Python is very powerful and can make its plot look exactly like R’s plot!
This gives you a sense of the “swiss army knife” of Python

title: Lecture 01
text:
The “Formula” vs. “The Matrix”
In R, a statistical model is treated like a scientific hypothesis. In Python, a statistical model is treated like “how does the computer wants its input formatted?”

R Approach: You use formulas (y ~ x). This is like saying “I think \(y\) changes in response to \(x\).” R automatically handles things creating the underlying matrix and keeps the names of your variables intact so you can read the results.
Python Approach: Most Python libraries(toolkits) require you to manually transform your data into a matrix of numbers first. Then pass them in as \(x\) and \(y\).

In R, the code looks like the math inside your head. In Python, the code looks like the way the computer understands math.

title: Lecture 01
text:
R v Python Example 2
R allows for a more linear flow of thought, less engineering, more thinking. Not good or bad, just a different philosophy. In each of these examples, we filter (subset/split up), aggregate (combine), then analyze:

RPythonPython with pandasPython one line


R uses the “pipe” operator (%>% Tidyverse library or |> core R) which is read like “then”. You know zero R today, but with a little help, you can read your R code like a sentence.
library(dplyr)                    # a library is like a toolbox filled with helpful functions
df %>%                            # df stands for "data frame", you'll learn more about this data structure soon 
  filter(year > 2020) %>%         # filter() function - keep these years in the data frame
  group_by(state) %>%             # Then, "group the data by" state for analysis
  summarize(mean_yield = mean(y)) # Finally, calculate the mean() save it to a new variable mean_yield
We created a new variable just by naming it.


In Python, you frequently create “intermediate” variables or use complex nested brackets to do the same:
from collections import defaultdict

## filter
filtered = [row for row in data if row["year"] > 2020]

## group and accumulate sums and counts
sums = defaultdict(float)
counts = defaultdict(int)

for row in filtered:
    state = row["state"]
    y = row["y"]
    sums[state] += y
    counts[state] += 1

## compute means
mean_yield_by_state = {
    state: sums[state] / counts[state]
    for state in sums
}

## print the result
for state, mean_yield in mean_yield_by_state.items():
    print(state, mean_yield)


This is why pandas exists (compare Python using pandas against the previous Python no pandas)
import pandas as pd

## assume df is a data frame in Python
result = (
    df[df["year"] > 2020]          ## Keep these years
      .groupby("state", as_index=False) ## aggregate by state  
      .agg(mean_yield=("y", "mean"))  ## Calculate the mean of y and store as mean_yield
)

print(result)


Python pandas is still readable even when complex
import pandas as pd

result = df[df["year"] > 2020].groupby("state")["y"].mean().reset_index(name="mean_yield")

title: Lecture 01
text:
Where are we?

Focus on becoming a “System Architect” who understands how the code (regardless of the specific language) serves a specific business or research goal (this AI cannot do yet). It is like study/ understand the process in addition to trusting it.
Focus on possessing AI Augmentation Skills – where AI is used as a tool to help humans do more, rather than replace humans. When coding in this class, AI is your helper to develop your computational thinking and broaden your understanding of the application of the code beyond the problem in front of us.
AI is the best at “book learning” so instead of competeting at that level – leverage AI to help you gain practical, hands-on experience through projects and then internships and then jobs. Show that you can apply what you have learned in the areas/industries/fields that you want to join.
Develop your Human Judgment - roles that require judgment, for example - handling complex client interactions, dealing with “messiness” (when things do not go as planned). Develop your Spidey Senses.

title: Lecture 01
text:
The Value of Computational Thinking



Decomposition - Breaking a larger problem down into smaller pieces
Pattern Recognition - Looking for similarities within and across problems
Abstraction - Avoid hyperfocusing on granular details and focusing instead on developing general solutions
Algorithm Design - Automating the process efficiently, ensuring reproducibility and reducing the need for excessive human intervention





Image created by ISTE & CSTA

title: Lecture 01
text:
Decomposition

Basic StructureAnd Still More


By the end of the quarter, instead of simply saying “I analyzed some data,” we can articulate more of what is involved as we learn how to do decompose what we do while learn R:

I read some data
I prepared the data for analysis
I generated statistics and visualizations
I modeled outcomes
I communicated my findings to others



and learn a little about a complete/professional workflow:

Ingest data (read CSV / JSON / SQL database)
Clean & make data consistent (e.g. fix various date formats)
Address missing values
Recode categories (regroup/relabel values)
Transform values (logarithms, standardization)
Engineer new variables (great creative skills)
Aggregate or Reshape/restructure data
Model / analyze the cleaned data
Validate/verify/reproduce results
Communicate results (tables, figures, reports)
Return to previous steps to refine one’s understanding (iterative)

Each step is clear and repeatable across different data & problems

title: Lecture 01
text:
Pattern Recognition
Intuitively seeking structure, repetition, regularity in data:

noticing the same data-cleaning steps apply to many different types of data files
recognizing that bootstrapping, permutation tests, and cross-validation share a common resampling pattern (upper division)
seeing that multiple models differ only by a formula or parameter

This is where the need for loops, reusable functions, and pipelines (making raw data analyzable) arise.
If I have time, the streetwise soldier who intuition saved his platoon during the worst of the Vietnam War (1965-1973).

title: Lecture 01
text:
Abstraction
Focus on what matters, minimize what does not:

data is “rows = cases, columns = variables” rather than obsessing over file format
thinking in terms of distributions rather than individual observations
defining a function that works for “any dataset”

Abstraction is what helps you generalize from one analysis to the next. This helps maximize productivity and minimize time spent in repetitive tasks.

title: Lecture 01
text:
Algorithmic thinking, good design
Create a clear, step-by-step procedure that produces a (reproducible) result

an iterative fitting routine
simulation steps (“repeat 10,000 times…”)
a reproducible analysis script that always gives the same output from the same input

This is the bridge between statistical reasoning and actual computation.

title: Lecture 01
text:
Why do this?
The American Statistical Association emphasizes computational thinking because modern statistics is no longer just formulas on paper:

Simulation > closed-form solutions (formulas)
Resampling (let the data tell us) > asymptotics (trust the math)
Reproducible pipelines > one time calculations/analyses
Data wrangling > textbook-clean datasets

statistical thinking + computational thinking = data science.

title: Lecture 01
text:
Workflow in Action & computational thinking

Decomposition is like the flow of data and thought from problem to solution
Pattern recognition is like seeing that flow across different projects
Abstraction is like “cleaning” & “modeling” & “reporting” generally
Algorithmic thinking is about having ordered, executable steps

Computational Thinking forces us to stop thinking in terms of isolated/one-off projects and start thinking in terms reproducible processes and the enterprise (whatever it may be) as a whole

title: Week 1 Getting Started
text:
First Steps: R the Calculator
R is a sophisticated calculator. Try the basic calculations in the code chunk below, just click Run Code when you are ready. You can modify the code and try different calculations too. Parentheses will work as expected, and R follows the standard order of operations (PEMDAS). Please try it.

Please enable JavaScript to experience the dynamic code cell content on this page.
What you might notice is that R isn’t storing the results anywhere except to print the results to your screen so you can see it (notice, you don’t need to type print() to see the results). The [1] that you see printed is just an index that R uses to indicate the position of the first element in the output. Since we are just doing simple calculations and there is only one element in the output, it is indexed as [1]. If you were to do a calculation that resulted in multiple values, you would see multiple indices.
R also uses new lines to separate the outputs of different calculations (or complete each expression generally). When you run the code chunk above, you will also see the results of each calculation on a new line.
If you want to save the results, you need to assign them to a variable (think math). You can use the assignment operator (read “gets”) <- to associate a value (name) with a variable. Try it out below.

But you don’t see any results when you run the code right? That’s because you are just associating the values with the variables named x, y, and z. If you want to see the results, in R, you can just type the variable name and run it.

title: Week 1 Getting Started
text:
Built-in datasets in R
No one is going to hire you to program calculations like the ones above, but they will hire you to work with data. R has a lot of built-in data that you can use to practice your data manipulation and analysis skills.
Let’s examine iris which is a built-in data set. You can run the code chunk below to see what it looks like.

Please enable JavaScript to experience the dynamic code cell content on this page.
Let’s unpack this! You can modify my code above in the browser, try modifying the box above with head(iris) instead of just iris and see what happens. head() is a function.
Functions
Functions do all of the work in R. Functions have a function name followed by parentheses. Functions can have arguments and options within the parentheses. So head(iris) reveals the first few rows of the built-in data iris. This is a way to get a quick look at the data without overwhelming you (or anyone else) with all 150 rows.
Examine iris
Notice the row numbering on the left and the column names at the top. The row numbering is just for reference and is not part of the data. By convention, rows typically (not always) represent an observation. The column names are important because they tell you what each column represents. In this case, we have measurements of different parts of the iris flower (sepal length, sepal width, petal length, petal width) and the species of the flower.
A handy function when you are starting out in R is is() (seriously). It tells you what is this iris thing?
An object is something that R recognizes and knows how to store it in memory and work with when you request the R object by its name. iris is a built-in R object that contains data. We can ask R what type of R object iris is:

title: Week 1 Getting Started
text:
The vector
In the example of x, y and z, a numeric vector is a sequence of values that are all of the same type (in this case, numbers). In R, the vector (there are different types, later…) is the fundamental data structure.
Notice that for a single number, R still treats it as a vector of length 1 (there are no scalars in R) with index [1]. This is a common source of confusion for those new to R. R is 1-indexed, meaning enumeration starts at 1. It is like the way we count. Python, C / C++, Java, JavaScript and many other programming languages are 0-indexed, meaning enumeration starts at 0.
You can examine the built-in data set rivers to see an example of a numeric vector. Try it out below and notice the values of the indices between the [].

Please enable JavaScript to experience the dynamic code cell content on this page.
How many values are in the rivers data set? You can check your answer by using the length() function or (for understanding only) by looking at the indices of the last value in rivers.

title: Week 1 Getting Started
text:
Back to iris
Remember iris above? It is a data frame, which is a more complex type of R object that consists of multiple vectors (columns) that can be of different types (numbers, characters, etc.). Another handy basic function in R is str() which gives you a quick overview of the structure of an R object. Try it on iris.

Please enable JavaScript to experience the dynamic code cell content on this page.
Now we are getting a real look at data in R. We see that iris has 150 rows and 5 columns. The first four columns are numeric (the measurements of the flowers) and the last column is a factor (the species of the flower). We will learn more about factors later, but for now, just know that it is a way to store non-numeric (categorical) data (like species).
I am going to leave you with two more useful basic functions, summary(), which gives you a quick summary of an R object. Try it on iris and just for fun, try it on rivers too. What happens and why?

Please enable JavaScript to experience the dynamic code cell content on this page.
and finally help() which gives you the documentation for a function or a built in data set like rivers or iris. Try it on head() to see what head() can do and what additional arguments it can take.

title: Week 1 Getting Started
text:
Takeaways

R is a fancy calculator that can do basic arithmetic and more complex calculations. Issue a help("Syntax") to see the syntax for basic calculations in R.
R uses line breaks to separate the outputs of different calculations (or complete each expression generally).

You can give a value a name (called a variable, like math), and then use that name (variable) in calculations and to store results.
R has many built-in data sets such as iris and rivers that you can use to practice your data manipulation and analysis skills.
Functions do all of the work in R. They have arguments that you can modify to get different results. For example, head() is a function that takes an R (typically) data object as an argument (it can take other kinds of R objects).
The is() function tells you what type of R object you are working with.
The vector is the most basic type of data object in R, and it is a sequence of values that are all of the same type.
The data frame is a more complex type of R object that consists of multiple vectors (columns) that can be of different types (numbers, factors, etc.).
R vectors are 1-indexed (numbered starting with 1), even when the vector only has one value (there are no scalars in R, only vectors).
The str() function gives you a quick overview of the structure of an R object.
The summary() function gives you a quick summary of the data in each vector (column) of a data frame.

A Data Science Workflow







From Google




From CRAN (the Comprehensive R Archive Network):

R is a system for statistical computation and graphics. It consists of a language plus a run-time environment with graphics, a debugger, access to certain system functions, and the ability to run programs stored in script files.

Translation:

R is a language with an interpreter and a standard library (toolkit/toolbox of functions)
With execution support code (behind the scenes code that helps your R code run on your computer)
All for the practice of statistics (involves computation,simulation, data visualization etc.)

R can also monitor/analyze code, identify coding errors, interact with your operating system, run programs saved on your computer as scripts (or similar) among other things.

title: Lecture 01
text:
Why R and not Python?

The basic difference: R was built by statisticians for statisticians, so the focus is narrower.
Python was built by software engineers for general purpose applications, so the focus is broad.
R is great for focusing on thinking about statistical problems, solving them, and communicating the results
Python is great for doing lots of different things. Example, download thousands of YouTube videos, analyze the images frame by frame, transcribe the sound into words, analyze the data, etc.

title: Lecture 01
text:
Why R and not Python? (cont’d)

R is “Problem-First” or “Problem-Forward”
In R, data structures are integrated directly into the language and do not require additional tools (but tools, found in libraries, are helpful).
When you load a dataset, R assumes you want to analyze it. The syntax is designed to mirror the way a researcher thinks: “Take this data, then filter it, then group it, then summarize the mean, etc.”

Also R’s simpler modeling formulas allows one to remain thinking about the analytical problem.

title: Lecture 01
text:
Why R and not Python? (cont’d)

Python is “System-First”
In Python, you “build” your environment before you can solve the problem (importing tools, found in libraries such as pandas, numpy, etc.)
In Python, it matters how the code integrates within a larger system, the result is versatility. So it is easy for Python to interact with YouTube for example (not as easy/or maybe not possible in R)
In R, what matters is how the programming code helps you reveals the truth in the data.

title: Lecture 01
text:
The “Formula” vs. “The Matrix”
In R, a statistical model is treated like a scientific hypothesis. In Python, it is treated like how the computer wants its input formatted.

R Approach: You use formulas (y ~ x). This is like saying “I think \(y\) is a function of \(x\).” R automatically handles things like creating “dummy variables” for categorical information (e.g., turning “Species” into 0s and 1s) and keeps the names of your variables intact so you can read the results.
Python Approach: Most Python libraries require you to manually transform your data into a matrix of numbers first. You then “One-Hot Encode” your categories and strip away the column names, then pass them in as \(x\) and \(y\).

In R, the code looks like the math inside your head. In Python, the code looks like the way the computer understands math.

title: A note on R objects and their names
text: This section was taken from “Advanced R” by Hadley Wickham (chief scientist at Posit, the creators of RStudio). Only the most essential part was taken from his book on this subject. While I use the word “gets” in a first Stats 20 lecture to help make it more accessible, technically, that day one explanation of the “<-” isn’t quite accurate and if you plan to do any advanced R programming in the future, it is best to make it as clear as possible from the begining. My notes and comments are in a different color - magenta

title: A note on R objects and their names
text:
from Chapter 2.2 “Binding Basics”
Consider this code:

x <- c(1, 2, 3)

It’s easy to read it as: “create an object named ‘x’, containing the values 1, 2, and 3”. ( or R object ‘x’ gets the vector 1, 2, 3 ) Unfortunately, that’s a simplification that will lead to inaccurate predictions about what R is actually doing behind the scenes. It’s more accurate to say that this code is doing two things:

It’s creating an object, a vector of values, c(1, 2, 3).
And it’s binding (associating) that object to a name, x.

In other words, the object, or value, (technically) doesn’t have a name; it’s actually the name x here that has a value 1, 2, 3.
To further clarify this distinction, I’ll draw diagrams like this:








The name, x, is drawn with a rounded rectangle. It has an arrow that points to (or binds or references) the value, the vector c(1, 2, 3). The arrow points in opposite direction to the assignment arrow: <- creates a binding from the name on the left-hand side to the object on the right-hand side.
Thus, you can think of a name as a reference to a value. For example, if you run this code, you don’t get another copy of the value c(1, 2, 3), you get another binding to the existing object:

y <- x









You might have noticed that the value c(1, 2, 3) has a label: 0x74b. While the vector doesn’t have a name, I’ll occasionally need to refer to an object independent of its bindings. To make that possible, I’ll label values with a unique identifier. These identifiers have a special form that looks like the object’s memory “address”, i.e. the location in memory where the object is stored. But because the actual memory addresses changes every time the code is run, we use these identifiers instead.
You can access an object’s identifier with lobstr::obj_addr(). Doing so allows you to see that both x and y point to the same identifier:

obj_addr(x)

[1] "0x128cf6e88"

obj_addr(y)

[1] "0x128cf6e88"


These identifiers are long, and change every time you restart R.
It can take some time to get your head around the distinction between names and values, but understanding this is really helpful in functional programming where functions can have different names in different contexts.
(end Wickham)

title: A note on R objects and their names
text:
The result of R’s ways
So take a look at what happens when we modify one but not the other

y[[3]] <- 4   ## I am following Wickham's style here, 

## instead you could have used y[3] <- 4 
## read as "y's third element" gets 4
## because we have simple vector, in other places 
## y[[3]] <- 4 is clearer, but we're not there yet

x

[1] 1 2 3

y

[1] 1 2 4


let’s check the memory locations

obj_addr(x)

[1] "0x128cf6e88"

obj_addr(y)

[1] "0x111dc5518"


(start Wickham again)
Modifying y clearly didn’t modify x. So what happened to the shared binding? While the value associated with y changed, the original object did not. Instead, R created a new object, 0xcd2, a copy of 0x74b with one value changed, then rebound y to that object.








This behaviour is called copy-on-modify. Understanding it will radically improve your intuition about the performance of R code.
(end Wickham)
Do you need to completely understand this to do well in Stats 20? Probably not BUT if you decide to learn Python or become a paid R programmer later (because all of the documentation assumes you understand R’s decision making in memory), it would help to understand what he is trying to tell you in Chapter 2 of the textbook Advanced R.
